example_summary: Mr. Bhargava received a ₹ 5 lacs professional fee to create a trust; the Supreme Court held this as an application of income, making it fully taxable under Section 28.
source_provision:
### Statutory Matrix: Diversion vs. Application of Income

| Characterization | Pre-existing Legal Obligation | Reaches Assessee First? | Tax Treatment | Benchmark Precedent |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Diversion of Income** | Yes (Overriding Title at Source) | No | **Exempt** (Not Income of Assessee) | *CIT v. Sitaldas Tirathdas (SC)* |
| **Application of Income** | No (Obligation created after receipt/accrual) | Yes | **Fully Taxable** under applicable Head | *CIT v. Thakar Das Bhargava (SC)* |


### Statutory Judicial Tests

* **Test of Diversion (Overriding Title):** An obligation must directly bind the **source of income** before it accrues to or is received by the assessee, diverting the revenue stream to a third party.
* **Test of Application:** Income first accrues to or is received by the assessee as their legal entitlement. Any subsequent transfer, charity, or payment—even under a binding personal contract or self-imposed obligation—is a mere application of income.


> [!IMPORTANT]
> **PGBP Impact u/s 28:** Professional fees or business earnings received by an assessee are taxable under Profits and Gains of Business or Profession upon accrual or receipt. The creation of a trust or charitable obligation by the assessee out of earned income does not convert an application into a diversion.

director.justification: The core question turns on whether professional fees received by Mr. Bhargava to create a trust represent a diversion of income by overriding title or a mere application of income under Section 28.
